utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to all. May we begin in the usual manner by taking the appearances for the day, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, assisted by Crispian Smith, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume the usher has gone to escort the witness back to the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Vlaski. Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to continue I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vlaski.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We will resume where we left off yesterday late afternoon. Both I and Mr. Zecevic asked you about the press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can the witness, please, be shown Exhibit 1D116, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, we unfortunately don't have the binder you had yesterday, so perhaps you can use the transcript you have in front of you. Or perhaps we have it. This will make it easier for you, since the print is rather small. Or, rather, bigger on the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I didn't switch my microphone on. Can you please look at that third passage from the top. I think it's tab 12 in your binder. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "By creating an anti-army atmosphere which can be deduced from the written order of the MUP for the police to be involved in the takeover of the military records from the JNA" -- I'm sorry that's behind tab 12. Would you agree with me that this constituted a rather large problem because the Muslim leadership of the MUP, in fact, was pushing the MUP into a conflict with the JNA, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is discussed in the context of the takeover of the records in order for military formations to be created that would be capable of confronting the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, within the MUP and state security hierarchy you were supposed to take up a rather senior post, practically that of the deputy, and correct me if I'm wrong, deputy under-secretary?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, deputy under-secretary. Nominally speaking, that's man number two within security structure, such as that of the Security Service. In other words, the man who would be ranked first and would be in charge of operative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So none of the operations -- none of the operative work could be decided upon or launched without consulting you or without the proposal coming from you. Were you not the one to propose the operative plan and the measures for its implementation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was envisaged under the legislation in effect and the bylaws governing the work of the service. However, the practice was never, or rather, the regulations were never put into practice because efforts were made for no one to occupy that post. It was a deliberate bypassing of a chain and a deliberate attempt to avoid the implementations of the laws on the part of those who wanted to act unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Within the lines of duties of an incumbent on that post, there were also measures of surveillance wire-tapping and observing the activities of an individual.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's only one part of it. No external or internal activity could have been planned without previous notification of the incumbent of that post. There didn't exist an opportunity for such a post to be abolished, formally and legally speaking, or that anything should be done in practice without the knowledge of the incumbent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You would have been the one, in fact, if it was necessary to adopt -- to take any measures of wire-tapping for the request to that extent to be forwarded by you to the higher-ups in order for this to be approved and implemented?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but only for justified reasons which need be presented by every person requesting any measure, including the measure of surveillance. In other words, any other measure which may encroach upon human rights and constitutional powers. Nobody could have embarked on such an activity without consulting the hierarchy, and it had to go from the lowest level up to the highest. The decision-making process had to start from the level at which a difficulty or a problem arose which requires the application of such a measure. So the first stage had to be first gone through where the problem was identified, measures proposed, and then one would address the -- the next immediate higher level and then what would follow would be the third filter and that would be the senior staff of the service who would decide whether the measures proposed were, in fact, commensurate with the threat which was posed and then from then on, the procedure would ensue as per regulations of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the post was abolished and that the SDA leadership refused to agree to your appointment to that post, this particular chain was fully bypassed by then and an alternative channel was set up with the help of which they listened in to individuals they thought were interesting to them.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a drastic example of unlawfulness which definitely required someone's consent or even a prior plan envisaging such activity. Even if the case had involved anybody else where the intention was to bypass laws, regulations, and certain levels, this would have been possible just as in any other service but, of course, there would have been a greater threat for the person to be uncovered in his unlawful conduct. In the circumstances as they were, there was no such danger for the person to be either uncovered or to be sanctioned for that conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, the Prosecutor asked you yesterday to confirm that you had recognised the voices of certain individuals. I'm interested in the specific case you discussed yesterday. Before the Prosecutor, or the investigator, played the audiotape to you, you were shown the transcript of the intercepted conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which particular transcripts or intercepts you're referring to, so I can't tell you, but I was given the opportunity to see the transcripts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up exhibit -- or rather, 65 ter 1056 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is the alleged conversation between Stojan Zupljanin and Mico Stanisic. When the Prosecutor interviewed you, you were shown the transcript, and you commented on it. For everybody's reference that's on page 17 of your interview. There you commented on this transcript. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I commented on this and other transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It follows from the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Krgovic. Are you referring to page 17 of the old one or the one where there was a correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the old version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll have to look for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the portion where you saw that it was a conversation between Zupljanin and then Gvozden and then you saw all the various names involved in the intercept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then as you arrived here, you listened to the audio of the intercept and the fact that you had previously seen the transcript helped you identify the individuals in -- concerned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not that much. I -- I really could recognise the voices and the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, this fact did facilitate the recognition of the individuals involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure whereby you were first shown the transcript stating the individuals involved and then played the tape is definitely not based on the police technique of identification as you applied it in your work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used to have problems in our work where interlocutors would speak without introducing themselves, but we had -- now there are certain techniques and methods whereby you can uncover their identities, whereas, at the time, we used other techniques and methods for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before you were played the audio, you commented on the transcript with the Prosecutor in great detail; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular transcript, the telephone number that was wire-tape is missing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was missing in all the other transcripts I was shown too. I wasn't paying attention to the telephone numbers or to the way the transcripts were labelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is indispensable in order for the telephone line that was wire-tapped to be established, and this would have then been done by the rules.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this should definitely have been mentioned in an Official Note which would normally accompany such material. As for the way we worked, it was customary for us to know which particular line was wire-tapped and on which date, as well as all the other elements necessary for the identification of the individual, place, and time, as well as other important elements for incrimination or for the substance of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The -- the start time and end time of the tape or the wire-tapping was not mentioned here; is that right? And that's important.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, time is important because technology enables us to define precisely the time at which certain things were done. And, for the purposes of any sort of police work, time is an essential element.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a few of the elements you've now mentioned and which should have been contained in such a document are missing from the transcript; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are. It says here telephone surveilled, but it doesn't say which one. Then the code number of the phone, well, there could be several technological possibilities of surveillance. The conversation could have been intercepted in a certain venue and then it is important also to know the device that was used and based on which the information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there is no note explaining on the basis of what elements Mico Stanisic was identified as one of the interlocutors because he was not -- his name was not mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the author of the analytical note. Maybe it is based on experience or his own knowledge of the voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the author of the analytical note should also indicate from what time the conversation was recorded?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, context is very important. If you are reflecting a conversation in its entirety then you have to include everything without deletion or redaction. If something is modified, that opens room for manipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from your experience in that period, do you know that these wire-taps were brought to the MUP seat, various sources were there compiled and then submitted to your service?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this type of work, the person who wants to provide a certain report based on these technical sources, the report can combine all kinds of sources, can put forward one single telephone check or use a combination of various sources, but the report should show that. And the person who receives that report cannot then use -- know exactly which sources were -- were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the second page of this document, please, where Zupljanin allegedly says: "Is there Vito, is Vito around?" The only Vito you knew was Vito Zepinic, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a normal way of reference and in conversation. Nobody called him with his full name, Vitomir. They always addressed him as Vito, everybody in the MUP and even further afield knew that it was Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, this type of work, wire-tapping of telephones without including this important elements and indication of sources, was unlawful and improper.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's unlawful in every respect. It's unlawful for one service to keep tabs on -- on their own colleagues from another service, and it is even more inappropriate to keep tabs on a -- on the chief of that other service. It's beyond the pale to arrogate the right to keep tabs on a colleague. It is a huge responsibility to assume, to get involved in such serious violation of the regulations. It only speaks about the people who were occupying such high positions at the time. And, also, it speaks to the absences of all checks and balances that should exist in a normal society. There should be checks and balances by the civilian authorities but also by the parliament because this service is supposed to be in the service of citizens, not only the people who appointed these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this transcript and what we see, the absence of these important elements, leaves a lot of room for manipulation, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my many years in the Security Service, including this type of work, that was always a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vlaski. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I re-examine, I do have an application to make, which I'm afraid will require the witness to leave Court. He does actually understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, the usher will escort you out of court for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may not be surprised to hear me apply regrettably for the second time in this trial to be allowed to cross-examine this witness in re-examination and treat him as a hostile witness. Every part of the evidence he gave evidence yesterday could be described virtually as adverse to the Prosecution case. All -- some of it actually volunteered, I can take Your Honours through the various parts. A lot came out as a result of leading questions but even more volunteered by him including the allegation - perhaps I better read it to Your Honours - that the total destruction of the state was intended by Mr. Izetbegovic and others. Your Honours, it's at -- of the transcript, page 638. The questioning was about the intercepts and the legality thereof. And he was asked by Mr. Zecevic about information being provided to the media, and then he talked about Sarajevo Oslobodjenje. "When you say involved, they were used for the purposes of a propaganda war, was it not? "A. Yes, it was part of the political, military, and media preparations for the takeover of power in Bosnia by the HDZ, SDA coalition and to the detriment of the Serb people. The representatives of this particular policy believed that they ought to be the masters in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It seems that for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the relationship between the master and the servant was a historical category and they believed that it was time for them to become the masters." He then went on to talk about -- he was actually being shown the various document with the complaints, and he then said that: "Mr. Kvesic, the head of the State Security Service, privatised the service. When he no longer felt he needed to remain in Sarajevo, he brought along with him documentation containing the service, if I may add, it was precisely because of such actions that were taken that certain individuals committed suicide." Then he went on to say -- I don't know how much longer I need to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, from Ms. Korner's comments just now, I really see no grounds for considering the witness hostile at this moment. I see no grounds for it in his answers to the Prosecution and to me -- to the Defence. He is a Prosecution witness. He was interviewed by the Prosecution and proofed here. If the Prosecution has failed to ask all the questions that were necessary to elicit the witness's real views and opinions, then it's their omission. I really see nothing hostile to the Prosecution in -- in the witness's evidence. He stated his views and his experience the way he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, I believe this Prosecution application is -- comes too late. The Prosecution could have, if they were unhappy with the witness's answers in direct examination, stopped their examination and asked to cross-examine the witness as hostile. Now, only after our successful cross-examination, are they coming up with this request, which I believe is contrary to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... hear you on Mr. Krgovic's last point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly. There is no bar to applying to treat a witness as hostile in re-examination. Although he said things and Your Honours may have seen that questions because I -- I'm sorry, I will start the sentence again. He was unforthcoming in examination-in-chief, which he was not in the course of the interview. If you recall the question I asked him in respect of why the meeting of the 11th of February was held in Banja Luka, he volunteered the information in interview that it was because it was a Serb-controlled municipality. I'll give Your Honours the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We remember [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, right. But, Your Honours I felt at that stage I didn't have sufficient to say that although he said a great deal which was not contained in the interview in which he was asked to give his account without leading questions, he never, for example, said, over and over again, as he did in this court, that the murder of the Serb wedding guest was a political murder. He gave an account which simply described it as a murder. I decided at that stage I would leave matters as they were. However, as a result of the -- the cross-examination, any lingering doubt that I may have had, that he was hostile, or adverse to the Prosecution case, was dispelled. He certainly never said in-chief this business of the destruction. I didn't read the further bit, but he said -- if he could call it a state. If Your Honours just forgive me, it's -- and therefore, yes. It is a caricature of a state, he called it. And that's at page 6391, all of which was volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my understanding of the status of hostile witness the way I had an opportunity to see it before this court, is that if the witness changes his evidence in a major way, either in -- compared to prior statements or to prior testimony, then he can be considered a hostile witness. Here, there is no major deviation either from evidence in direct or in -- in cross-examination. There is no major shift that could justify his treatment as hostile witness at this point. And this is, on top of everything, a viva voce witness, and what he said in direct, he repeated in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The application that the Office of the Prosecutor has made to treat the witness called by them as an adverse witness and so as to permit counsel to cross-examine that witness in the course of her re-examination is an application which the Chamber grants, because it is patent from the record that the tone and the -- sorry, not tone, but the -- the overall effect of the witness's testimony was that, as the Prosecution now advances, in essence, adverse. And the appearance of this, and I pause to select the right word, the appearance of this in the course of examination-in-chief became obvious in the course of cross-examination so that the practical footing on which the application is made is from a perusal of the record obvious. There are certain procedural issues which may arise, because it is exceptionally an application being made while the Prosecution is about to re-examine -- re-examine, and not as would ordinarily happen while the witness was being examined in -- in-chief. We expect that that may be cured by allowing the counsel for each of the accused limited time to further cross-examination -- to further cross-examine after Ms. Korner would have completed her re-examination. The -- and, therefore, we would, upon the witness being invited to return to the stand, allow Ms. Korner to proceed in the manner that she has sought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness comes in, I would appreciate a clarification. Does your decision mean that the Prosecution's cross-examination and the topics would be limited to our cross-examination? Because that would be fair, not to allow the Prosecution to go beyond the topics that we discussed in cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. I have no intention of going outside what was raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That solves the problem [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, the Chamber has made a ruling that although you would have been called at the instance of counsel for the Prosecution, at this stage of their reexamination, counsel is being permitted to cross-examine you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski before we deal with some of the matters of principle, if I can put it that way, that you raised in your answers, can we just go back to a moment for the intercept that you listened to between Zupljanin and Stanisic. When you came to the Tribunal on Sunday, you listened to the intercepts, did you not, before you were shown any of the transcripts and the other documents?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did listen to the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You listened to them without the benefit of having any transcripts in front of you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when I was listening, I didn't have the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And you have no doubt at all, as you've told Mr. Krgovic, whether or not you saw the transcript eight months ago in Banja Luka that the voices that you heard on that intercept are those of Stojan Zupljanin and Mico Stanisic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't go into any analysis. My aim was just to identify the voices, and since I'm in full possession of my capacities, I was able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what you told this Court in one of your many lengthy speeches yesterday was that what was happening was that there was a: "... political, military, and media preparations for the takeover of power in Bosnia by the HDZ/SDA coalition and to the detriment of the Serb people. The representatives of this particular policy believed that they ought to be the masters in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It seems that for Bosnia-Herzegovina the relationship between the master and the servant was a historical category, and they believed that it was time for them to become the masters." That's what you believe, is it, Mr. Vlaski?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gained that impression from my personal experience and from the general situation on the political scene, in the media, and in the security services. It was my impression that there was a plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're saying that from reading the newspapers, from the general situation on the political scene, and -- can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is -- is a misinterpretation what the witness said. He said three things: The security situation; the media; and the political scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. But I think you're only asking him for two things and he says based on all three things he had that impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You know, I'm quite sure that the witness doesn't need Mr. Zecevic's help. Your Honour, I'm taking this in stages. I'm asking for an explanation of what he means by "the political scene."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I will answer the question. The political scene in Bosnia-Herzegovina was defined by the BH constitution. The constitute nature of the peoples is that they are the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina and representatives of these three peoples won the elections, and it was only natural and it so happened that after the first multi-party elections they set about forming the government. However, following the elections, the HDZ/SDA coalition was formed, and it was symbolically represented through the binding of the two flags together. So the representative of the Serb people found themselves confronted with a two-to-one ratio where two stood for the majority of the Bosniaks and Croats. And everything was determined on that majority. The political situation was such that the parliament where democratic decisions were to be taken and where the constituent nature of the peoples was to be respected, became the forum of outvoting to the detriment of the Serbian minority. This manifested itself also through the decisions of the government, although the constitution dictated that a consensus and an agreement among the three peoples should take place. I could hold a speech on this topic, but if this will suffice, I can end it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would really love to know what you call a speech. I'm so sorry, you say that they were outvoted in the -- everything was determined by the majority. Isn't that a democracy, Mr. Vlaski?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a democracy, according to the western standards where a mono-ethnic states are concerned, but in a multi-ethnic state such as Bosnia-Herzegovina was where the constitution dictated a consensus and an agreement among the constituent peoples, it is not governed by that particular principle. One element or one ethnic community had to be content with the situation. Lacking that, the democratic principle was not met.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the transcript does not reflect what the witness said, and I feel it is important even for -- for Ms. Korner so I don't how to deal. Shall we ask that the -- that -- that -- that the tape be listened again. But it doesn't -- it wouldn't help Ms. Korner or maybe he should slowly repeat what he said word by word because the transcript says something which is -- which is definitely not what he said. And I think it is an important issue about the constitutional specificity in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Vlaski, without counsel for the Prosecution having to repeat her last question, could you give us your answer again and perhaps sufficiently slowly so that it can be adequately interpreted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't think that my emotions can be easily controlled in situations such as these so I tend to speak more quickly, but I will try to do it more slowly. The constitutional position of Bosnia-Herzegovina is defined as a community of three constituent peoples where all three peoples take key decisions by way of a consensus. In other words, the constitution does not provide for a possibility of outvoting on the part of a democratic majority as in other democratic states in the west and elsewhere. But Bosnia-Herzegovina is a multi-ethnic state, and it rests on this principle of multi-ethnicity and constituent nature of peoples. This is part and parcel of the constitutional provisions that outvoting shall not take place. In order for the interests of every single peoples to be respected, they have to have this mechanism enshrined in the constitution in order for them to protect their national ethnic interests. We're not talking about a civic state, you're talking about a multi-ethnic state, so these are peoples who have the fortune or misfortune of living in the same country in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the community came into existence based on the willingness of the three peoples to live together. However, at some point, there arose a difficulty where the three peoples didn't want to live anymore together so that that's why the constitution envisaged the provision where for key decisions to be taken, the agreement of even the smallest people had to be achieved and -- and down to the last citizen of the country whose rights had to be guaranteed. In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the principle was violated because a coalition was created between the party of democratic action and the Croatian democratic union, and it manifested itself politically through the binding together of their flags and in the parliament through the outvoting and taking of decisions against the will of the Serb people represented in these organs of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The third element that you said led you to take this view was the -- your personal experience, general -- sorry, in the media, the security services. Are you referring there to what you describe as the - I'm trying to think of the right word for it - the seizing of the key positions by Muslims and Croats and not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle of the separation of power implies a distribution of power on an equal footing according to the significance. You can't allocate to someone a higher level post and to others to be street cleaners. What was essential was to allocate down the hierarchy political posts and positions in the government. In order for the power to be distributed according to the interparty agreement. The interparty agreement was achieved, and it only needed to be implemented. This was not supposed to be the subject of bartering or trading off. If an agreement is achieved, it can either be implemented or not. The Serbs agreed to this interparty agreement even though it was to their detriment because they did not have this historical experience of what was important, which leaders of power were important to be held so that even in this area they gave the advantage to the representatives of the majority people including the Croat people who admittedly were not the majority people. It is important -- it isn't important who will be occupying which post if the constitution and the laws are being respected. If the regulations are applicable to all then they will be duty-bound to implement them. However, the problem arises when individuals claim right -- their right to decide which post is important and which is not and when they enjoy political protection in doing so. And they claim the right to decide which post should not be occupied for certain individuals in order for them to realise their plan. And that was the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that a deliberate obstruction was taking place in order for the Serb people to be tricked politically and otherwise in order for them to be bypassed and in order for time to be gained. Once power is established, it is very difficult to change the structure. As for the security sector, they covered literally all the positions and did what they wanted. They did not feel the need to ask or consult anyone on any matters let alone the representatives of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I must express again. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is your view if I understand you correctly from what you said before and what you say again that the Serbs were inexperienced, didn't realise what was happening until too late; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to the Serbs. I was referring to the political leadership of the SDS and their naivete. I'm -- as for the intentions, they may have had the best of the intentions when they took up the positions of the minister of information, the minister of agriculture, health care, or science. These were the posts that they fought for, the Speaker of the parliament. Now as for the prime minister, minister of foreign affairs, minister of the interior, the presiding of the Presidency, these were important posts which the Serbs did not occupy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's deal with the political leadership of the SDS, shall we? Were you aware that on the 14th of October, 1990 something called the Serbian National Council was established by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This appeared from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The whole tenor of his answers, volunteered in answer to leading was that the Serbs were naive and had reacted too late. In addition, he was asked about -- in a document produced by the Defence, the SDA setting up a National Defence Council in June of 1991. This arises directly out of those questions, not Mr. Krgovic's, I accept, but certainly Mr. Zecevic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with what you have been asserting, were you aware of something called the Serbian National Council being established in October, the 13th of October, to be precise, 1990?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain that it was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can I show you -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, because this all came up today. It says Oslobodjenje -- again, we haven't got it in e-court, but we -- and nor indeed has it got an ERN number, but it -- can I just finish then, it was referred to in a footnote in Dr. Nielsen's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we already cross, I think, the line in some respect with -- leaving the Prosecution the right to -- to cross-examine the witness during the re-direct and then ultimately giving the opportunity to the Defence to re -- recross-examine. Now, this is -- is -- as I -- I -- I have to accept that this is the ruling of the Trial Chamber. I have my opinion on that, but what I think is, if Ms. Korner is allowed to use some additional documents, which have not been used, which have not been noted in -- in their -- in their exchanges that they are going to use with this witness, then we are -- we are -- we are going way out of bounds, in my modest opinion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, but can I just be heard on this before you make a ruling? The document the Defence produced, as you appreciate, we have never seen before. We have no idea even if they are genuine in connection with the SDA. One in particular, a huge point was made about the fact that in June of 1991 the SDA had set up what was called a National Defence Council, and we don't have what it refers to because we haven't been provided with the accompanying declaration. In addition to that, this witness has said over and over again the Serbs were at a complete disadvantage because they were naive and only reacted too late. I'm therefore entitled to put in re-examination, aspects, particularly now I've been given leave to cross-examine, of evidence which is available to the Defence because it is referred to, as I say in a footnote of Dr. Nielsen's report that show what he has said is not supported by available evidence. And that's the submission I make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me. We notified the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution in accordance with the Rules rendered by the Trial Chamber in this case of the documents we would be using. These were Defence documents, and documents to be found in e-court. Now, the fact that Ms. Korner saw them for the first time, I'm really sorry about that, but that's her problem, really. She had them for two days when the witness took an oath, and then we disclosed the documents. She had a whole day to review the documents and to submit her opinion on them. The fact that the document was disclosed by the Defence as a document on the basis of which the witness would be cross-examined has nothing to do with what I'm saying, and that's that the Prosecution cannot be now allowed to use documents that they have not announced, that were not used either in the examination-in-chief or in the cross-examination. And that is my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The documents were only released to us when the examination-in-chief began. I did look at them. Indeed, I sent Mr. Zecevic an e-mail about my objections to them, and you heard us argue them yesterday. What I'm saying is that we've got no chance of checking these documents at all when we only get them at the beginning of examination-in-chief. Which, if we're lucky, we get half a day to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that Mr. -- that it would essentially uphold Mr. Seselj's objection and allow the Prosecution to put questions but without putting -- putting -- referring the witness to a particular document, that simply would invite complications that we needn't bring on ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm perfectly prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, it's a minor mistake in typing. It's page 25, line 10. I think instead of Mr. Seselj, it should be Mr. Zecevic maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vlaski. Can I put it to you, for your comments, you have obviously heard because you say you don't think it was in October of 1990 that the SDS did establish a Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a member of the SDS. According to the working practice within the police, we were not required to analyse the work of the political structures. Perhaps it was somebody's duty to analyse what the SDS was doing, but we didn't have the official duty to do so because nobody told us officially that we should be occupied with that. So I wasn't aware of the fact that they had such a body, but I did know there was a political council of the SDS which gathered intellectuals who supported the party but were not members of it. I know of such individuals indirectly that they were involved in the work of that council. Now, as for this particular council, I'm not sure what its name is. Well, what I find important is the activity performed by a certain body, its activity or even more importantly inactivity. I don't know what this body was doing, so I can't give a position on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me suggest to you that the founding of this council was published in the newspapers, including Oslobodjenje. Karadzic was its first president, and the text of the decision, let me suggest to you, said as follows: "The council will be made up not only of parts of the republican SDS leadership but also of representatives of other parties and even independent, distinguished persons. The first decision of the council was adopted, by which the Serbian people make it known that it will not recognise any decisions on the change of the BiH state unless it is arrived at through a referendum of the Serbian people." Now, do you remember reading anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a great deal of such things and we were practically swamped by them. Now as for the text itself, I can't say that I am familiar with it, but I am familiar with the context. I was of the general political position that the Serb people, as a constituent people, had the right to speak their mind on this very important issue, such as the constitution in form of a state. Initially the -- initially Yugoslavia and later on Bosnia-Herzegovina because of their constituent nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You know, just for the purposes of the record, I should add it was Oslobodjenje on the 14th of October in which this was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: 1991. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1990. Your Honour, that's the point I'm putting to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Vlaski, if that's right, then the SDS, the leadership, was already making its position absolutely clear way back in 1990. Wasn't it? It wasn't reacting to things.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a position in relation to the future of the state because what was discussed at the -- at that point was Yugoslavia. We were under the constitution of Yugoslavia, part of it. You forget that there was the federal constitution which was binding on the republics forming the state, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that's quite clear. From this particular document, the article in the Oslobodjenje concerning this position, well, there is nothing strange about it because all the peoples are called upon to protect the constitution, to safe-guard the constitution. Is it a disgrace to try and safe-guard the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll try one more time, Mr. Vlaski, and we'll move on. The point that I'm seeking to see whether you will accept is that contrary to what you assert that the SDS leadership didn't appreciate what was happening and was only reacting to things too late. Right from an early stage, Mr. Karadzic was making it clear that the SDS would make sure that the rights of the Serbian people were protected.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a legitimate demand from a representative of the Serbian people even if it was Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll move on to the next topic. You spent a little time explaining to Mr. Zecevic -- just let me get the page number from yesterday. It's at page 6421. This is one of your lengthy speeches. It started at page 6420, and it was put to you by Mr. Zecevic that one of the tactics which was pervasive, particularly prominent in the minister of the interior, was to postpone and drag the resolution of certain issues that were raised by the Serb side. And I think this was in the context of an intercept. And in the course of this long answer, you said this, you raised the Badinter Commission, and then you said: "If this was an option that we were going to be given," the role of a national minority, that is, "... it is clear that Izetbegovic received political and international support to organise a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina" which, by the way, you added was never verified by any of the institutions. This particular act, which was organised in Bosnia and Herzegovina without the participation of the Serb people, and this was counter-constitutional, had never been verified by the BH organs. In -- on the 4th and 5th of November of 1991, was a plebescite organised by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a referendum, a plebescite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You want to draw the distinction, do you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a terminological difference and a difference in substance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you vote in that plebescite?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I voted for the existing constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that envisaged equality for both republics and the peoples. We had lived in such community until then, and there was nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that, if you were a Serb you received one colour of a polling card; if you were a non-Serb, you received a different colour?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about such details. I just went to cast my vote. I didn't particularly look at the polling card to see the colour or appearance. I just came to express my will, and what kind of paper it was printed on, I didn't care.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't read anything from the SDA or any of the other national parties pointing out that there were different coloured ballots, whether you were a Serb or a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can a -- someone coming to the polling box be recognised by ethnicity? Who would make that sort of distinction and identification of people by pushing one sort of paper or another into their hand? It's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Bosnia it's fairly easy, is it not, to distinguish -- I --

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's extremely difficult, in fact. Not anymore perhaps because people change the way they dress and sometimes they're very easy to identify nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you had the -- never mind. Let's not get into an argument about this. So you're saying you're unaware of this. Were the results of this plebescite ever given any kind of -- let me find the express you used -- any kind of verification by anybody?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not institutionally organised or prescribed by law and constitution as a procedure. It was an initiative by a political party. It did not go through the institutions, and there was no need for it to be officially verified. It was not something organised by the authorities. It was organised by a political party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you know, don't you, that the results of this plebescite were used as the basis, the authority, for the founding of the Serbian state in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I think this is a complete -- completely untrue. We all know how Republika Srpska came into existence. This sort of misrepresentation of facts is inappropriate, I would say. I would be grateful if Ms. Korner could rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, maybe -- I'm going to find the document -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. If Your Honours would take the break now, I'll get the document that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have asked for document 65 ter 1259 to be put up on the screen when the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not objecting. I'm just stating for the record that this has not been notified to the any of the parties that this document will be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't going to use -- I just told him -- I only brought this because Mr. Zecevic raised the objection to what I was putting to the witness and said I was misleading him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I -- I'm under the impression but perhaps I'm wrong and then I should adapt my system. But I'm under the impression that you used in your cross-examination some documents as well that weren't on the list that you gave us before we came in court. You think I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm 100 percent positive, Your Honour, that you are wrong. I don't know how it happened but it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For instance 1D-- 1D14. I didn't see that on your list. It's an exhibit -- exhibited document, that I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But I didn't see it on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the documents were listed, plus we added a few documents during the -- the direct examination and we notified the parties on that. On all the documents. I will -- I will -- I will check out the -- the -- the mail and I will inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I missed an e-mail. That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that document 65 ter 1259 is put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I assume while we're waiting, Mr. Vlaski, you remember the declaration on proclaiming the republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 9th of January; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the preamble to this. "In order to contribute to the peaceful and agreeable resolving of issues related to the territorial boundary determination and other rights and duties related to achieving the right on self-determination of the Muslim and Croatian people in the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina as lawful representatives elected in a free and democratic way and protector of its rights and interests, implementing its will expressed by plebescite and its decision based on the plebescite to establish the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." Now, you complained - and this is the only reason I'm putting this to you, Mr. Vlaski - that the referendum held in March was not valid, not ratified; but the same is true, is it not, of the plebescite which had, may I suggest to you, even less validity than the referendum?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't have less validity. A plebescite was just the expression of the will of one people organised by one political party. A referendum, on the contrary, is an act by the authorities, by the state, that has to meet the requirements of both form and substance to make a decision that will include the consent of the Serbian people, and without that consent there could be no referendum and that was the key point in this case. A referendum could not be held without the consent of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In some other states perhaps it would have been possible. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, however, it wasn't. And it was an anti-constitutional step.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't consider, do I take it, Mr. Vlaski, that setting up the -- the Serbian -- the republic of the Serbian people within Bosnia in January was in any way an unlawful or anti-constitutional step?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a declaration, an expression of volition. It's nothing official. Here in the preamble it says that every attempt will be made to achieve a peaceful agreement-based solution. You know well that the international community was by this time was involved in the solution in attempts to solve this problem. All the peoples in Yugoslavia enjoyed this right to self-determination. If everybody enjoyed it, why not the Serbs? And the same goes for Bosnia-Herzegovina because in Bosnia-Herzegovina Serbs are also one of the constituent peoples. Why should they be treated any different from other peoples? Why shouldn't they have that right? I think they have that right and they must enjoy it and they must be able to exercise it if they live in a well-ordered state ruled by the law. We had no other law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you accept that this action by the SDS in declaring the state and everything that followed thereafter, if nothing else, contributed to the outbreak of violence in April?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not the reason. The SDS, apart from this political aspect of its activity, had no other element to it that would point to its involvement or organisation in preparations for any conflict. Because the Cutileiro Agreement was precisely along the lines of the decision of this decision by the Assembly of the Serbian people, that the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina should agree about their rights and obligations, and also about the territories and try to find a model which would be a solution. And that agreement was agreed upon, although there were no guarantees by the international community that it would be implemented, and it was very naive of the Serbian people not to have required any guarantees from the international sponsors. And precisely because there were no guarantees, this agreement was violated eventually precisely by those who reckoned they had enough power to make decisions without taking into account the Serbs, and that's why we ended up forming these regions that were known later as SAO Krajina or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question again. Would you accept that this action by the Serbs, the SDS, in 1992, the founding of the Serb republic, contributed - and I emphasise contributed - to the outbreak of hostilities in April?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered the question. It did not contribute to it. This was a political action. It was all legitimate and all these declarations. There was nothing final about it, it was just an expression of a political attitude, a political decision that had to be harmonised yet and agreed upon with other peoples. If you decide something, it doesn't mean that it is carved in stone that it will bear no further modification, but it was something for the future. There was room for negotiation yet and for agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll move on. You were asked about -- by both counsel for the Defence, again, about the 11th of February meeting. And it was put to you in terms by Mr. Zecevic - just let me find the right place - that no one could suggest -- I better just get the right words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I thought I had marked up the place but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that Mr. Zecevic, if I get it wrong -- he put it to you in terms that this was not a secret meeting and you agreed wholeheartedly that the meeting in Banja Luka -- yes, I've got it. It is page 6423. And he put to you: "That was not a secret meeting, was it?" And you said: "No, it was in no way a secret meeting. I can absolutely claim that it was not a secret meeting of any type." If it was not a secret meeting, why was it held in the hotel Bosna and not in the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely because it was not a secret meeting. You can go into the CSB building, you can go into the CSB building only if you're authorised, but hotel Bosna is a public place, a public venue. Anyone can walk in. And it's not secret also because the conclusions from this meeting were sent to Delimustafic, the minister. Why would that be done if the deliberations were secret? It's absurd to claim there was any conspiracy to it. These transcripts were not meant for Serbian leaders and Serbian policemen, they were offered to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a proposal for -- for a way to resolve the many problems that had accumulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, should we have look at what you told us in interview about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please, page 30, and this is the revised version, whether the names and the like were corrected. So, sorry, 65 ter 9020. Is there a B/C/S version? I'm afraid, Your Honours, there's only an English version, but the interpreters can see it then. It's page -- it says 30 of 73 at the bottom, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have been asked on the previous page to look at the minutes of the meeting, and you were asked as I asked you whether they were accurate and you said, for the most part, yes. And then you were asked: "Did you take" - top of the page - "any contemporaneous notes like an agenda? "No, by that time, I had already given up on writing any notes. I don't have any notes from that meeting. We were all -- we actually arrived unprepared to the meeting. The chiefs of the CSBs, the centres, they had the real power especially here in Banja Luka where the Serbs were in the majority and they actually had the power. In Sarajevo, we were illegals." And then do you remember who asked you to the meeting, and you said, "Dragan Devedlaka ... I don't know who informed whom, but it is logical to me that Dragan Devedlaka would have hierarchically have been informed by whoever, Mandic or Stanisic. "And these minutes, were they distributed to the participants after the meeting? "I don't think I got it." And the investigator said: "Okay. Because you looked at it less than a minute and you knew all about this meeting. I just wondered had you ever seen this document before today? "Later on, I did see it. I don't know if it was Radovic or Zugic. I think it was Goran Radovic who gave it to me." So the minutes were not distributed immediately after the meeting, is that right, Mr. Vlaski?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the records were there, the people who prepared the meetings and organised it and prepared the records had all these technical things under control, and we who travelled to Banja Luka had to return to wherever we came from, so I'm not so familiar with these transcripts. I was not in such a position as to deserve a transcript. I could, for instance, receive one from Mr. Zedlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what the witness actually said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- if you can help Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He said that somebody who organised and prepared the meeting had the records and had to deal with them in a technical way. I assume he meant that has to be retyped or something like that. But the -- the -- the -- the transcript says all these technical things under control which is -- which means nothing, and that is precisely the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if I can put it -- so what you're saying, and tell me if is this right, please, Mr. Vlaski - I don't want to put words in your mouth - is that you had nothing to do with how the minutes were produced. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, the recording secretary takes the record in this case, this is Mr. Belasevic, and he is the person who was responsible for what is in the transcript, in the minutes. And I said, I believe it reflects the atmosphere and the topics of the meeting, although you can't see from this that there was any secret or a meeting organised in advance because there were no invitations or an agenda notified in advance because the first prerequisite for a properly organised meeting is to inform everyone of what the agenda would be. We did not need an agenda, to be fair, because we had only one topic to discuss, the issue of survival. And the records were done later, because we had no laptops and we had no typewriters. I don't know where they did it physically, where they prepared it. I was not familiar with the technical aspects of this job and who formulated these minutes and these conclusions. Perhaps they could be arranged better, in a different order, and perhaps they could be even formulated better, but that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... line 6, it says -- Ms. Korner said "the minutes" and it says in the transcript "the manipulates" were produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vlaski, I don't want to get too bogged down in that, but I would like to move now to what you then dealt with. You say -- you were asked by the investigator: "Can you recall these conclusions" -- can we push the page up a bit? Thanks. "Can you recall these conclusions?" And you say: "No, I believe they were compiled later. "How long did the meeting last? "Can't tell you. "Why held in Banja Luka?" And can we go to the next page, please. "I don't know who insisted on being in Banja Luka, I don't know who organised it all." "Would you call it a closed meeting," said the investigator? "Mr. Zupljanin provided security. We didn't feel insecure where personal security was concerned. I believe this meeting could have been held anywhere. I don't know who organised it and why Banja Luka was picked. "Q. But this was a meeting only open to Serb police officers not to Croat or Muslim." Your response: "Yes, and that was his intention." Now do you still say this wasn't a secret meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It absolutely was not secret. I don't see why it should have been secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if it wasn't meant to be a secret meeting and you wanted to make your feelings known to the Muslims and Croats that you said were taking all the positions, why didn't you invite them to this meeting? Why didn't you have Mr. Delimustafic to this meeting with Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic and express your grievances?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really, I have to -- you make me laugh. They -- they should have come to our meeting. Well, they didn't call us to the meetings where they should have called us because we were part and parcel of the authorities. Were their partners in the everyday work that was supposed to be performed. They didn't call us to these meetings we were supposed to attend, and it would have been ridiculous for us to think that they would come to one meeting that we organised, and it wasn't really logical for them to be invited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you absolutely reject any suggestion that this was a meeting that was to be kept quiet from the other nationalities in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first meeting, and I've already said that. It was on this occasion that I met many of the people for the first time and got to know them. We hadn't had any previous communication unlike the representatives of the Bosniak and Croat peoples who had everything at their disposal from the various vehicles to communication devices and premises. They didn't invite us to their meetings, and this became only too apparent from everything that happened later. So this entire process had lasted by that time for a year. Had we acted responsibly towards ourselves, then we should have by the 11th of February, been very familiar with one another and communicated our positions to one another. But the fact that on the 11th of February we only met many of the people amongst ourselves, only goes to show that we were at the very beginning of any activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the time of this meeting, perhaps you'd like to go to the minutes and could we have them up on the screen again. It's 1D -- have you got them in your -- 1D135. By the time of this meeting, the Assembly of the Serbian Republic had already made a decision on -- that there was to be a Serbian MUP established, hadn't it? That's what Mr. Radovic says.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's what it should state because that's what the declaration was as well as the political position that the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And Mr. Stanisic, in his speech that we see on that page, talked about the Council of Ministers of that Assembly, didn't he? First line: "The position of the Council of Ministers at the last session was that the territories in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which are under Serbian control, that control must be felt ..." So he was talking, wasn't he, about the Council of Ministers of that Assembly, of which you may or may not have known he was a member?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an advisor. He had the role of a political representative of sorts of the MUP within the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and his political role was to co-ordinate the work of MUP representatives in -- or rather, to co-ordinate the work of the MUP with the representatives of the MUP of Bosniak and Croat ethnicities and to co-ordinate the work with the Council of Ministers which was set up at the Assembly and the SDS. From his presentation it is clear that the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina is being divided by the Muslims and not by the Serbs. To us, this was common knowledge. Their statements to the public at large and all the other activities they undertook were aimed at laying all the blame at the Serbs, so the result was the formation of the Serb MUP from the municipal level to the regional level to the ministry itself, but this was only a -- a -- a project at its inception at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can I ask my original question again. Were you aware, and it seems that you were, that Mr. Stanisic was a member of the Council of Ministers of the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't want to object because there has been so many objections already. I just don't see how this comes out of the cross-examination, and I will beg Ms. Korner to pay attention to the limitation that has to be imposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was asked both by -- by both counsel about the content of these minutes, and his assertion is that at all times the minutes were -- it was intended and that the minutes were sent to Mr. Izetbegovic, and I'm just dealing with that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- I beg your attention just -- He was asked on direct about the minutes of the 11th of February meeting. He was re -- cross-examined, examined exactly on that basis because he was asked on -- this document was produced to him during the direct. He was cross-examined during the cross-examination on the same document. I don't see how, out of our cross-examination, anything of the sort that -- that refers to the Council of Ministers or anything comes out. I'm 100 percent sure that I never asked this question nor has Defence of Zupljanin, or anything remotely connected to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to go on asking unless you tell me -- I've got just one point to make, and I would like to make it, if you allow me. If you don't, then I won't. There has been cross-examination on this document. I appreciate I opened up in examination-in-chief, but I want to explore some of those replies in re-examination, in particular the assertion that these minutes went to Mr. Izetbegovic, which is not something I think that was said in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were you also aware - before I move onto the next point - that Mr. Stanisic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. In particular the certification that these went to Mr. Izetbegovic which was not something that was said in-chief. I heard Ms. Korner saying Izetbegovic. This is a misinterpretation. He said the minutes -- he said in direct in the cross-examination that the minutes are going to Delimustafic, the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant Mr. Delimustafic. I said Izetbegovic, but I meant Mr. Delimustafic, which I apologise, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now maybe we can finish this topic fairly quickly. Were you aware that not only was he a member of the Council of Ministers but a member of the SDS, a founding member it appears?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really, because I was not in charge of the personnel policy of the SDS nor was I interested in the work of that party in that sense as to who was a member or who was not. As for the work of the Council of Ministers I was interested in that because that was a process that had been launched, and I knew that he was involved in the work of the Council of Ministers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic says: "A list of minimal outstanding demands should be assembled at this meeting and submitted to Minister Alija Delimustafic." Correct? Do you see that? It's Mr. Stanisic 's speech. It may be on the next page in B/C/S. You are asserting, do I understand this, not that a list of demands was sent to Mr. Delimustafic but these minutes of this meeting in Banja Luka; is that what you're saying? I just want to understand that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the form itself was not that important. The intentions were important. The format could have been that the message could have been conveyed verbally or in writing. What mattered was the intention to acquaint Mr. Delimustafic who was nominally the minister and who was the individual who dealt with these matters was informed of this. We believed in the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We only thought that the conduct had to change, and that's why it mattered that the document be sent to Mr. Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, look, Mr. Vlaski, you have shown us over and over again you're not a stupid man. You know the difference between a list of demands being send and the minutes of a meeting such as this. I want to know, the Trial Chamber may want to know what are you saying? Are you saying that these minutes, these typed-up minutes were sent to Mr. Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim either way because I don't know who was supposed to formulate and convey the demands. This is not stated in the minutes, and I was not informed of it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because the only person, the only people who are said to be informed of the conclusions, if you go to number 18, if we can go to the fifth page in English and probably about the same in B/C/S. Yes. Are -- it says: "Inform the Council of Ministers of the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it has nothing to do with the objection. It is the translation problem. And ministerial council. It says in the original [B/C/S spoken] of the mentioned conclusions the Council of Ministers is to be informed too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's difference is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe the difference is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The English should say: "Of the above conclusions, the Council of Ministers should also be informed," or something along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure you're right, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I want to ask you about these minutes. And finally, can we turn one last time to the question of intercepts about which you have had so much to say. As I understand your complaint, it is that the intercepts which were made, in particular of Mr. Karadzic, were illegal and particularly illegal -- and other people, other Serbs, because the operatives used were not, at the time, members of the MUP. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided an analysis of the procedure. The request for the application of any measures has to be based on some sort of information. In this case, orders for the application of measures and the entire procedure starts from the top and runs along illegal channels that were outside of the institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if I may have a moment. Ms. Korner, I know that Mr. Krgovic spent quite a bit of time on this, but the -- need you go down this road? Because the question of the legality of this trial -- this trial -- is this really something that the Chamber at the end of the day is going to have to consider?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, well, I mean -- but, Your Honour, I don't know is the answer because I know that you have ruled on this, as it were, but it wasn't really Mr. Krgovic. It was more Mr. Zecevic who spent a very long time and put various names to him, as to the operatives. So I'm dealing with that as much as I can. But if Your Honours, as we will be submitting that -- the -- the legality or otherwise is not something that -- that will make these intercepts admissible or non-admissible then I'm perfectly happy to leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, of course I'm not going to anticipate what eventual conclusion the Chamber might reach. I only say that in the context of the clear ruling -- rulings, I think there are more than one, that the Chamber has given that I'm surprised that counsel on either side felt the need to go down this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's -- may I say, Your Honours didn't stop Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Krgovic, so I can't read Your Honours' minds, can I? I feel I ought to deal with this slightly in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think that over the months sometimes the -- I think counsel on both side would have appreciated that the, speaking for myself, perhaps my fellow Judges as well, but rather that intervening in -- when counsel is on a particular plank, the preferable course is to say nothing in the hope that it would -- that he would come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It goes away [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm perfectly happy to leave it, I mean, being given that indication. I hope I won't, if it later comes to argument, be put at a disadvantage because I do have certain matters I can put to him about it. But I'll -- I will take Your Honours' guidance on this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
